Title: Goldman Sachs earnings: 'The bad news is out,' analyst says
Text: [Goldman Sachs shares are on the rise despite reporting a Q2 profit miss. Wells Fargo Managing Director Mike Mayo sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to detail his outlook on Goldman Sachs as the banking institution pivots away from consumer services and CEO David Solomon's vision comes into question. Mayo shares his opinion on banking leadership succession plans while stating Goldman Sachs may have had its "second-worst quarter" under Solomon's helm, while excluding the pandemic years.Video Transcript- Goldman Sachs rounding out second quarter earnings season from the big banks and, well, it wasn't pretty. Profits tanked 58%, hit by write downs in the company's consumer and asset management businesses. Embattled CEO, David Solomon, told investors on the conference call, he is confident in his strategy. But should investors be confident in David Solomon?Mike Mayo is Wells Fargo's managing director and head of US large cap bank research. Mike, always great to get some time with you, especially in studio. So David Solomon saying things might be OK, things might be getting better. Should investors believe him?MIKE MAYO: Well, let's do the short-term, medium-term, and long-term. The short-term is this is a situation of sell on the rumor and buy on the news. We had been expecting, in our numbers, big write downs. You got big write downs.And you, as a firm, can't have $1.1 billion write downs every quarter as you pivot away from consumer, as you pivot away from an acquisition-- they did Green sky-- as they pivot away from these on balance sheet investments. And by the way, a lot of write downs for office specifically. So that's what's happening now. So the bad news is out there in the stocks up today. In fact, I actually increased my estimates because you've got some of the bad stuff out.In the medium-term, it waits to be seen how soon the capital markets come back. You've had lower for longer investment banking, you've had less volatility for trading. So in some ways, it's the worst of all worlds. But the backlog is up at Goldman Sachs versus last quarter, and the question is, how much of that backlog do you convert and monetize to revenues?Story continuesBut the long-term is what's really the big question here is. And Goldman Sachs is going back to the future by getting out of consumer, which I thought was stupid day one. You go back, any research, any time I've been on your show, like, why were they--- He's using a Goldman Sachs credit card. I mean, this is Amex. This is Amex land. Mastercard, Visa.- I don't even mean that, I mean, like, the Marcus lending. You're going to lead off to the mass consumer in the United States with a lending product? Sure. That doesn't create sticky relationships. And then they go ahead and do that with a savings account by charging-- that doesn't create sticky relationships.By the way, look at JP Morgan in London. They lead with a checking account where you interact several times a day. That builds sticky relationships. So I thought I was stupid. And the more it went on, it was even more ridiculous. So better late than never to pivot away from this.But now, they're going back to the future. Their legacy over the past 150 years has been serving large institutions. So 2/3 of the company is global banking and markets, where they get mid-teens returns, they have number one leadership in mergers for 20 years, this quarter, equities did great. So that part of the business, nobody has too much question about.Another 1/3 of the company is wealth and asset management. They are doing better in the wealth business but they have to get rid of some of these principal investments, which is a big drag from a regulatory perspective. And then there are extracurricular activities and consumer and some of these other things that they're getting rid of.So they get rid of the stuff that's extracurricular, they stay in their lane, they pivot and make themselves more balance sheet efficient and more operationally efficient. And then if and when these green shoots materialize, maybe, they get from a lowly core-- their ROE this quarter was 4%.This was the second worst quarter under David Solomon, excluding the pandemic. It was the worst quarter in over seven years for Goldman Sachs. So this is bad. You can't keep doing this. But their goal is to take it from the 4%, or 9% adjusted for the charges, up to 15% over the next two to three years.I don't have that. No one in consensus seems to have that. So no one's really believing David Solomon. So the bar is low. They're not trading too far above book value for a company that's grown book value faster than most banks.So I think this is an opportunity. The risk is that it just stays kind of dead money as other things go up. But this is a big pivot. This is a big day for Goldman Sachs. David Solomon is under pressure. So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

Title: How Goldman Sachs earnings stacked up to rivals
Text: [Goldman Sachs second quarter earnings report saw a plunge in profits and missed expectations on both the top and bottom lines. Yahoo Finance Senior Reporter David Hollerith breaks down how the company's earnings compared to other big banks.Video Transcript- Well, profits plunged at Goldman Sachs during the second quarter. The Wall Street giant saw its investment banking revenue declined 20% from a year ago, and the impairment charges helped drag earnings down 58% to $1.2 billion for the quarter. So how does Goldman Sachs square up against some of the other big banks that we've seen this earnings season? Yahoo finance's David Hollerith is here to weigh in. David, please, take it away.DAVID HOLLERITH: Jared, so the call just finished up and CEO, David Solomon, he pointed out that it's been a very tough quarter but also did point to things to come that could be bright spots. Now, the bank has been telegraphing that it's trying to pivot its business, it's moving away from its one-time efforts to get into consumer lending and trying to focus more on its core business now.How it's stacked up this quarter to the other major banks, just if we're looking at more of the Wall Street-type revenues, which is trading and investment banking in particular, Goldman has shown better than expected results in trading or worse than expected results in investment banking. That's compared to a year ago, the drops.Now, Morgan Stanley has shown the worst in trading so far, and Citigroup has had the highest loss or drop change from a year ago in investment banking. As far as Goldman goes, it also had nearly $1 billion in one-time impairment charges or what the bank is trying to tell us has been a one-time impairment charge. And that was a focus on the call. Analyst, Mike Mayo, with wells Fargo was asking about that.And really, I think the question there is whether or not Green Sky, this company, this consumer lender that they purchased back in 2021 will be sold. And it does sound like that is happening, and that this will be sort of the end of the markdown. There are also severance charges too. So Goldman obviously is moving away, and it's trying to grow its asset management and wealth management businesses, which Solomon had said will take years to grow.Story continuesMorgan Stanley, obviously, a close competitor has been building its wealth management business for the past decade. And that obviously cushioned their revenues a lot, and it shows why they did not have quite the same amount of losses as Goldman has seen in this quarter.- Yeah, really interesting to track Goldman versus Morgan Stanley, because both of them only became banks over the global financial crisis. But I want to move on to something else, David. As more smaller and mid-sized banks are reporting earnings, something to watch out for is higher capital requirements. Jamie Dimon has been talking about that. And Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, Brian Sozzi, spoke with Bank of America Chairman, Brian Moynihan and CEO, what he expects for this sector. And let's take a listen to that.BRIAN MOYNIHAN: If you do this across the whole banking system and that's why we're all awaiting these rules. But we hope that as the rules come out, they're balanced in terms of international competition. In other words that right now, America and Europe appear to have the same rules, but they are advanced and weren't standardized. And if you listen, they're saying, well, we're going to go away from the models and all those things. That was the basis of Basel III to get to advanced.So our advanced RWA are $1.4 trillion, our standardized are $1.6, so we have to use a higher under America's rules. That's not true in other locations. And so we have to be careful about keeping the balance in the competitiveness of the US banking system, which is key not only to America, honestly, but it's key to the whole world because the strength of our banking system actually helps the world prosper.- So interesting words there, David. Your thoughts.DAVID HOLLERITH: Yeah, I mean, I think just to put it simply, the amount of capital that banks have to hold, that obviously controls how much they can actually make use of their money as opposed to holding it on hand in case of deposit changes. And I think that we're getting a lot of different regulatory results with the Fed stress tests that came out a few weeks ago, which sort of measured it, tested a different thing that was more for how banks held up during an economic recession.And what this is is this is more so a change for banks over $100 billion in assets to meet the standards that the biggest banks have. And so that's going to change a lot of what they can do with their capital. And we have to expect something like a long period for this rollout as with the big bank regulations that have been set in place since I guess they were established in 2018 and are still being rolled out. But the big banks are ahead as far as that goes.And we're looking at some banks in particular that are right on the cusp like US Bancorp. And they're in a more difficult position to do it. But there is a strategy for how they can sort of optimize their capital in such a way that it doesn't so much reduce how much they can lend. But that is obviously the concern here.- Yeah, it seems to me a lot of these big bank CEOs not necessarily liking the new capital requirements, but we'll see how it shakes out. Thank you for that report, David Hollerith.]

Title: Debt issuance 'a wildcard' for banking stocks: Analyst
Text: [Big bank profits seem to benefit the most from a higher interest rate environment in Q2 2023. Jon Curran, Principal Asset Management Portfolio Manager, outlines the impact debt and bond issuances have had on the financial sector. Following bank consolidations tied to the regional bank crisis in early 2023, Curran commented to look for "symbiotic deposit footprints that are complimentary in nature" where institutional banks seek out M&A activity.Video TranscriptDIANE KING HALL: Big banks have delivered their Q2 earnings. And the landscape is better than expected. Higher interest rates boosted the bottom line for many large lenders, though. Other income streams, like investment banking took a sizeable hit.So what's the smart financial play for your portfolio? Jon Curran, principal asset management portfolio manager, joining us now. So what is the smart play in light of all the results that we have received, Jon?JON CURRAN: Well, good morning. It's great to be with you. I think the smart play here is to stay in the large liquid diversified banks that have a nice blend of fee and interest income in their top line.I think the results really highlight the importance of diversification. And the big banks have shown themselves to be a bright spot. And that they're resilient. And their deft handling the deposit rates amidst the higher rates.JULIE HYMAN: Hey, John. It's Julie here. So in your portfolio, which of these do you hold the most of? Or what are you adding to right now?JON CURRAN: Well, we work on the bond side. And we look for the large liquid balance sheets, good access to funding, not just on the deposit side, but on the access to the debt markets. And one of the big surprises this year, one of the wild cards has been the debt issuance, which last year in 2022, January saw a $29 billion of debt issuance. This January is $9 billion.This quarter, really, is the first quarter of material bond issuance. And we've seen a lot of it. So we're looking for the banks that have durable deposit bases, but that also can access wholesale funding markets and have the investor receptivity that they do.Story continuesDIANE KING HALL: And Jon, then who would you be dumping in light of that when you use your investment thesis?JON CURRAN: So I think general good diligence wins the day here when you're considering bank investments. It's really important to do your homework, know the management teams, know that they're making good underwriting decisions. There are headwinds on the horizon. The recent fed loan officer survey did show some contraction in lending standards and lending overall.But the big banks have been very resilient in passing through some of those rates, in the form of loans to their customers while lagging the increase in deposits. They can do that because they're blessed with these large deposit bases.JULIE HYMAN: What about the non-big banks, Jon? We heard from some of the regionals today. And it looks like that, by and large, they're holding on, or even in some cases growing their deposit bases. They're having to pay up to do so. Is the debt of those banks as attractive?JON CURRAN: Well, I think I think you make a very good point. I think the recent results of the big banks really shows the widening gulf between the haves and the have-nots, the gigantic banks, the money center banks, which are positioned very well to withstand headwinds and any turbulence that may be coming down the pike, and the smaller regional banks.It was heartening to see some of the really large regional banks like PNC, Truist and US Bancorp come to market in June. That opened the gate for regional banks. But we haven't seen regional banks writ large be able to access the debt markets yet. So I think we need to just see a bit more earnings stability and a little bit more how firm or how well footed their deposit bases are before we get some sense that they can persist with success like their large bank peers.DIANE KING HALL: Jon, with more regulation coming down the pike, pretty much imminent, are you expecting to see more consolidation? And who do you see in the-- like we saw JP Morgan Chase getting bigger recently because of that consolidation. Who do you see being a target in that situation?JON CURRAN: It's an excellent question to see where the next tie-ups will occur. I think you have to look for symbiotic deposit footprints that are complementary in nature. You did see the 2019 merger between BB&T and Suntrust to form Truist. To have a transformational merger like that might make sense, but it will depend on where the deposit concentrations are the largest.But I think clearly, the large banks have shown themselves to be ones that can persevere through this environment. So the larger the banks, the more levers they have to pull, both in their top line and their funding businesses. And if you look at their concentration risks, commercial real estate is one of the headwinds out there for these banks. But the large money center banks are much more insulated. Not impervious, but more insulated than their smaller peers.JULIE HYMAN: What about just the general headwind as well from decrease in lending demand across the board, whether we're talking about businesses or individuals?JON CURRAN: We did see the contraction in some commercial and industrial, as we like to call it in the industry, C&I lending, the recent fed loan officer survey. I think that's clearly one of the headwinds that we've noted that's on the horizon.Nonetheless, JP Morgan and Wells Fargo did say that their earnings they expect to make from loans is increasing. So it's a bit of a-- on the one hand, there is probably some contraction ahead and some credit tightening. But on the other hand, there is still demand.Citigroup actually posted a surprisingly large jump in their credit card revenues. And they were the bellwether. The one thing you have to worry about or just be cautious about is if the more borrowing that occurs on plastic, the more the banks have in terms of their loans. So that's one thing we're watching, keeping a watchful eye on.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah. And indeed, we're seeing the provisioning for that kind of stuff start to creep back up once again. Jon, thanks for your perspective. Jon Curran, principal asset management portfolio manager. Appreciate it.]

Title: How banks, financial stocks could be the closest thing to a Q2 bellwether
Text: [Could bank stocks be the closest thing to a bellwether in Q2 2023 as earnings continue to roll out? Wells Fargo CIO of Wealth & Investment Management Darrell Cronk joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the state of the consumer and credit trends as reported by banks this week. In a note, Wells Fargo cited bank earnings to be illustrating the "true economy" while Fed officials reconsider future interest rate hikes and consumer spending remains consistent and resilient.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: While earnings season has just begun, it does seem like the bellwether this quarter is shaping up to be the financials despite the sector's earlier chaos this year. For more, we're joined by Darrell Cronk, Wells Fargo CIO of wealth and Investment Management.And indeed, it has been really interesting how well the financialS-- let's leave Goldman aside for a moment. But how well they've done. And can we sort of extrapolate that out to the rest of earnings season at all?DARELL CRONK: I'd be careful, probably about extrapolating. It out I think financials have exceeded-- what I've had my eye is very closely on is both what Brian just referenced, which is the consumer and the trends. So the consumer has been resilient. The consumer always remains resilient into a slowing economy.In fact, the consumer is often the last one to kind of give up the ghost, if you will. They will spend right up to the edge of potentially a recession and jump right over the cliff into it. We're starting to see some of that in the numbers.So if you go back to the pandemic. Huge amounts of transfer payments to consumers who built big savings balances. They've ground through those savings balances. Late last year early this year, we saw big increases in credit card spending. And now, just in the last month or two, credit card spending literally dried up.Like, it went just dead silent, which is often a very late cycle indicator because it means the consumer is kind of hitting the wall, right? If they don't have the savings anymore to spend and they can't use the plastic, right? Then they stop spending at some point.Story continuesSo I think it's a really important trend to watch. We're seeing in just this quarter's earnings. We're seeing credit card delinquencies rise from a very low level but rise, nonetheless. We're seeing auto delinquencies rise from a low level but rise nonetheless. So there are some trends there that they're watching. I think, directionally, even though they're not at the normal magnitude you would expect in a late-cycle event.DIANE KING HALL: So, I feel like that's kind of the glass empty-- or glass half-empty side of the equation. It could be the-- could it be though the glass half-full side of the equation when you think about just the strength of the labor market backing up that spending that we're seeing? Sure, there's a little bit of tapering we are seeing.But again, it's not the magnitude that you would expect in terms of like what we're seeing in the financials and how these banks are holding up. We're also not seeing massive outflows. What do you make of that?DARELL CRONK: Yeah, I think that's right, Diane. And I think we've got this air pocket of labor, both firms have been resilient and not wanting to let go of their high-valued employees. But coming out of the pandemic, we had 10 million job openings and six million unemployed workers, right?We've never seen an environment like that where there was that big of a mismatch. So it's not surprising that labor has remained sticky. Now, I think what you have to parse there is-- is it labor just being sticky and not rolling over or is it that companies are robustly out there hiring today?We don't see the robust hiring side. Call it the demand side of the equation. In fact, what you really need for that to kick in is you need earnings growth and you need top line revenue growth, right? So we're going to be the second quarter in a row of negative earnings revenue growth, third quarter of negative earnings growth, and the sixth quarter in a row where we've seen margins declined.So if that environment happens and demand comes down and your single biggest cost on your income statement is labor, you would expect that if it's typical to a normal cycle, in the coming months, those layoffs would start to pick up a little bit. But you're right, the resiliency has been has been really strong.JULIE HYMAN: But is it typical to a normal cycle? I mean, the thing that kind of comes around to me as we go through each earnings season. You know, we kept talking about normalization coming out of the pandemic. And then, the conversation goes away. But, really, we're still there.I mean, when you talk about the credit card delinquencies for example. They're ticking up but they're still below where they were in 2019, which is remarkable to me. And it feels like they're all still these tension points in the economy that are not normal. Whatever normal even means anymore.DARELL CRONK: That's true.JULIE HYMAN: Right? So--DARELL CRONK: You're right, Julie.JULIE HYMAN: We're still-- what is that process still like? And how difficult does it make your job and our job to try and figure out what's going to happen?DARELL CRONK: Very difficult, right? Because if you looked at a lot of the historical indicators and the fundamental indicators. You would basically say the economy is very late cycle and probably heading to recession, which is why you had 70% of economists claiming coming into this year that the economy was going to go into a recession.That intense bed of liquidity that we just got done talking about, probably extended the duration of how a number of those normally roll over and act. But at the end of the day, the consumer is the engine of the economy, right? And labor is what will matter there.What's interesting is-- so, we all know the Fed started hiking interest rates in March of 2022, right? Very first hike at 25 basis points. The unemployment rate in March of 2022 was 3.6%. The unemployment rate today is 3.6%, right?It hasn't moved. Notwithstanding the fed has increased interest rates 500 basis points, right? So does that mean labor is different this time or this time is different? Maybe. Where you see strength in the economy. I think the important point here is you have to parse is it supply push or demand pull? Because there are two different things.If it's-- so think about, we've seen strength in labor. We've seen strength in housing. We've seen strength in travel and all those types of things. So take housing for example. People aren't lining up to buy two and three new homes. That's not happening today, right?Why is housing strong? It's strong because there's such a supply dearth, right? There's only been 1% of homes turned over this year, right? Same thing with labor. There's a dearth of labor, right? It's not that companies are running out there to hire a whole bunch of new people.Same thing in travel, right? Airlines have done what? Cut the number of flights. So if you want to go to Europe, right? This summer, you're going to pay up because there aren't the seats there.JULIE HYMAN: In that case, it feels like there's quite a lot of demand for travel though too.DARELL CRONK: There is. There's pent up demand from the pandemic, right? People just want to get back out there and do their thing again. But it's kind of colliding with this reduction in supply of what's available for seats. If you go try to find a summer seat on an airline this summer, best of luck to you, right?DIANE KING HALL: Whoa, wow, OK, I have one more flight to get to.DARELL CRONK: Yes, OK, all right, sorry, Diane.DIANE KING HALL: I better book that today.DARELL CRONK: You better get that booked.DIANE KING HALL: Exactly.]

Title: Goldman Sachs earnings: 'The bad news is out,' analyst says
Text: [Goldman Sachs shares are on the rise despite reporting a Q2 profit miss. Wells Fargo Managing Director Mike Mayo sits down with Yahoo Finance Live to detail his outlook on Goldman Sachs as the banking institution pivots away from consumer services and CEO David Solomon's vision comes into question. Mayo shares his opinion on banking leadership succession plans while stating Goldman Sachs may have had its "second-worst quarter" under Solomon's helm, while excluding the pandemic years.Video Transcript- Goldman Sachs rounding out second quarter earnings season from the big banks and, well, it wasn't pretty. Profits tanked 58%, hit by write downs in the company's consumer and asset management businesses. Embattled CEO, David Solomon, told investors on the conference call, he is confident in his strategy. But should investors be confident in David Solomon?Mike Mayo is Wells Fargo's managing director and head of US large cap bank research. Mike, always great to get some time with you, especially in studio. So David Solomon saying things might be OK, things might be getting better. Should investors believe him?MIKE MAYO: Well, let's do the short-term, medium-term, and long-term. The short-term is this is a situation of sell on the rumor and buy on the news. We had been expecting, in our numbers, big write downs. You got big write downs.And you, as a firm, can't have $1.1 billion write downs every quarter as you pivot away from consumer, as you pivot away from an acquisition-- they did Green sky-- as they pivot away from these on balance sheet investments. And by the way, a lot of write downs for office specifically. So that's what's happening now. So the bad news is out there in the stocks up today. In fact, I actually increased my estimates because you've got some of the bad stuff out.In the medium-term, it waits to be seen how soon the capital markets come back. You've had lower for longer investment banking, you've had less volatility for trading. So in some ways, it's the worst of all worlds. But the backlog is up at Goldman Sachs versus last quarter, and the question is, how much of that backlog do you convert and monetize to revenues?Story continuesBut the long-term is what's really the big question here is. And Goldman Sachs is going back to the future by getting out of consumer, which I thought was stupid day one. You go back, any research, any time I've been on your show, like, why were they--- He's using a Goldman Sachs credit card. I mean, this is Amex. This is Amex land. Mastercard, Visa.- I don't even mean that, I mean, like, the Marcus lending. You're going to lead off to the mass consumer in the United States with a lending product? Sure. That doesn't create sticky relationships. And then they go ahead and do that with a savings account by charging-- that doesn't create sticky relationships.By the way, look at JP Morgan in London. They lead with a checking account where you interact several times a day. That builds sticky relationships. So I thought I was stupid. And the more it went on, it was even more ridiculous. So better late than never to pivot away from this.But now, they're going back to the future. Their legacy over the past 150 years has been serving large institutions. So 2/3 of the company is global banking and markets, where they get mid-teens returns, they have number one leadership in mergers for 20 years, this quarter, equities did great. So that part of the business, nobody has too much question about.Another 1/3 of the company is wealth and asset management. They are doing better in the wealth business but they have to get rid of some of these principal investments, which is a big drag from a regulatory perspective. And then there are extracurricular activities and consumer and some of these other things that they're getting rid of.So they get rid of the stuff that's extracurricular, they stay in their lane, they pivot and make themselves more balance sheet efficient and more operationally efficient. And then if and when these green shoots materialize, maybe, they get from a lowly core-- their ROE this quarter was 4%.This was the second worst quarter under David Solomon, excluding the pandemic. It was the worst quarter in over seven years for Goldman Sachs. So this is bad. You can't keep doing this. But their goal is to take it from the 4%, or 9% adjusted for the charges, up to 15% over the next two to three years.I don't have that. No one in consensus seems to have that. So no one's really believing David Solomon. So the bar is low. They're not trading too far above book value for a company that's grown book value faster than most banks.So I think this is an opportunity. The risk is that it just stays kind of dead money as other things go up. But this is a big pivot. This is a big day for Goldman Sachs. David Solomon is under pressure. So I think over the next year, we're going to have to see some signs that they're going toward that 15% return.- Mike, do you think Solomon is the right person for this job? Is he going to be able to steer Goldman in the right direction? Because there has been, like you just said, tremendous amount of pressure, not only from shareholders, but even within the firm, from partners who haven't been happy with the direction.MIKE MAYO: Well, look, like anyone else at Goldman Sachs, David Solomon has to earn the right to be in his job every day. I think from a strategic standpoint, this idea of focusing on two core businesses, pivoting out of the stuff that isn't so core is the right strategy.So really, it just comes down to execution. And can they execute on their plans. And that's why I'm here, that's why you're there, that's why all the eyes are there watching them quarter to quarter to quarter.So right now, David Solomon is still there. Actually, the stock price has outperformed since he's been there. Their capital markets activities grown much faster than the others since he's been there. They've exceeded book value faster. So on those metrics, it looks good. But I'm more concerned about the next three to five years.So, yes, David Solomon is the right person at the moment. But I'm still watching closely quarter by quarter by quarter.- Mike, I've followed your work, probably, for well over a decade, and there's been a theme during that decade. The leaders that are still operating this business, leading these companies as CEO, are still entrenched.Brian Moynihan, I talked to him yesterday, very much engaged. Doesn't sound like he's going anywhere anytime soon. Maybe Jamie Dimon finally bows out as CEO in the next two to three years. He's been teasing it for 10 years or whatever it is. Morgan Stanley seeing a change, and James Gorman in a year and a half. What has this current guard of CEOs meant to the financial services industry? And is the next crop of leaders, are they as good as these guys?MIKE MAYO: Well, these leaders were born out of the global financial crisis, which, as you recall, from 2008, 2009, was the biggest crisis since the Great Depression. And so they learned some pretty hard lessons. And so these are survivors from that crisis. And so what doesn't kill you makes you stronger.And that's certainly the case with Jamie Dimon, which bought Bear and WaMu during the global financial crisis. And then he comes back again and buys First Republic and acts as a leader. So look, I've had my spats with Jamie Dimon. And I just thought they were spending way too much a year and a half ago. And now they're showing incredible discipline.I mean, what company-- I mean, had an IPO on just now about beauty, right before oddity. I thought banks might be the-- that's the beauty, the banks are the beast, I guess. So today you have Beauty and the Beast.But, I mean, what company-- JP Morgan just guided for 10 billion higher in revenues between this quarter and last quarter, and guided for zero increase in expenses. That's amazing, after all the criticism I gave Jamie Dimon. So you're not going to find too many Jamie Dimons coming along.In terms of James Gorman, I said, in 2012-- I upgraded the stock-- I said, either stock price should go higher or he should be fired. And after that, James Gorman-- it was an inner day upgrade after they had a terrible fixed income quarter. James Gorman picks up the phone, calls me, I thought it was a joke at first. And the first reaction by him-- and he had his team, I had my team-- he said, so that wasn't very nice. And I said, well, I just think the stock should go higher. He goes, so do I. And let me tell you why I think it will.So this idea of not acting defensive-- you get red flags from people who act defensive. You see it on your show sometimes. But this was the opposite of acting defensive, being open-minded. So I think that sort of open mindedness-- you can have that, you might not have that. But when someone gets in the position, do they actually act that way?And Brian Moynihan, I also thought he should be fired. I went to a special shareholder meeting a decade ago and he proved me wrong. And frankly, I think I would have said the same thing a decade ago, I'm not sure he was ready to become CEO. But that's just grinded out quarter after quarter, year after year, build a better mousetrap.So I think they're all good in different ways. So there's definitely an opening for new leaders to emerge but they won't have been as battle tested as James Gorman, Brian Moynihan, or Jamie Dimon.- Point well taken. Mike Mayo, thanks for coming down on a very busy day for earnings. I know you have more to go. We appreciate it. It's a real treat.MIKE MAYO: Thanks for having me.- Thanks so much.]

Title: How Goldman Sachs earnings stacked up to rivals
Text: [Goldman Sachs second quarter earnings report saw a plunge in profits and missed expectations on both the top and bottom lines. Yahoo Finance Senior Reporter David Hollerith breaks down how the company's earnings compared to other big banks.Video Transcript- Well, profits plunged at Goldman Sachs during the second quarter. The Wall Street giant saw its investment banking revenue declined 20% from a year ago, and the impairment charges helped drag earnings down 58% to $1.2 billion for the quarter. So how does Goldman Sachs square up against some of the other big banks that we've seen this earnings season? Yahoo finance's David Hollerith is here to weigh in. David, please, take it away.DAVID HOLLERITH: Jared, so the call just finished up and CEO, David Solomon, he pointed out that it's been a very tough quarter but also did point to things to come that could be bright spots. Now, the bank has been telegraphing that it's trying to pivot its business, it's moving away from its one-time efforts to get into consumer lending and trying to focus more on its core business now.How it's stacked up this quarter to the other major banks, just if we're looking at more of the Wall Street-type revenues, which is trading and investment banking in particular, Goldman has shown better than expected results in trading or worse than expected results in investment banking. That's compared to a year ago, the drops.Now, Morgan Stanley has shown the worst in trading so far, and Citigroup has had the highest loss or drop change from a year ago in investment banking. As far as Goldman goes, it also had nearly $1 billion in one-time impairment charges or what the bank is trying to tell us has been a one-time impairment charge. And that was a focus on the call. Analyst, Mike Mayo, with wells Fargo was asking about that.And really, I think the question there is whether or not Green Sky, this company, this consumer lender that they purchased back in 2021 will be sold. And it does sound like that is happening, and that this will be sort of the end of the markdown. There are also severance charges too. So Goldman obviously is moving away, and it's trying to grow its asset management and wealth management businesses, which Solomon had said will take years to grow.Story continuesMorgan Stanley, obviously, a close competitor has been building its wealth management business for the past decade. And that obviously cushioned their revenues a lot, and it shows why they did not have quite the same amount of losses as Goldman has seen in this quarter.- Yeah, really interesting to track Goldman versus Morgan Stanley, because both of them only became banks over the global financial crisis. But I want to move on to something else, David. As more smaller and mid-sized banks are reporting earnings, something to watch out for is higher capital requirements. Jamie Dimon has been talking about that. And Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, Brian Sozzi, spoke with Bank of America Chairman, Brian Moynihan and CEO, what he expects for this sector. And let's take a listen to that.BRIAN MOYNIHAN: If you do this across the whole banking system and that's why we're all awaiting these rules. But we hope that as the rules come out, they're balanced in terms of international competition. In other words that right now, America and Europe appear to have the same rules, but they are advanced and weren't standardized. And if you listen, they're saying, well, we're going to go away from the models and all those things. That was the basis of Basel III to get to advanced.So our advanced RWA are $1.4 trillion, our standardized are $1.6, so we have to use a higher under America's rules. That's not true in other locations. And so we have to be careful about keeping the balance in the competitiveness of the US banking system, which is key not only to America, honestly, but it's key to the whole world because the strength of our banking system actually helps the world prosper.- So interesting words there, David. Your thoughts.DAVID HOLLERITH: Yeah, I mean, I think just to put it simply, the amount of capital that banks have to hold, that obviously controls how much they can actually make use of their money as opposed to holding it on hand in case of deposit changes. And I think that we're getting a lot of different regulatory results with the Fed stress tests that came out a few weeks ago, which sort of measured it, tested a different thing that was more for how banks held up during an economic recession.And what this is is this is more so a change for banks over $100 billion in assets to meet the standards that the biggest banks have. And so that's going to change a lot of what they can do with their capital. And we have to expect something like a long period for this rollout as with the big bank regulations that have been set in place since I guess they were established in 2018 and are still being rolled out. But the big banks are ahead as far as that goes.And we're looking at some banks in particular that are right on the cusp like US Bancorp. And they're in a more difficult position to do it. But there is a strategy for how they can sort of optimize their capital in such a way that it doesn't so much reduce how much they can lend. But that is obviously the concern here.- Yeah, it seems to me a lot of these big bank CEOs not necessarily liking the new capital requirements, but we'll see how it shakes out. Thank you for that report, David Hollerith.]

Title: Debt issuance 'a wildcard' for banking stocks: Analyst
Text: [Big bank profits seem to benefit the most from a higher interest rate environment in Q2 2023. Jon Curran, Principal Asset Management Portfolio Manager, outlines the impact debt and bond issuances have had on the financial sector. Following bank consolidations tied to the regional bank crisis in early 2023, Curran commented to look for "symbiotic deposit footprints that are complimentary in nature" where institutional banks seek out M&A activity.Video TranscriptDIANE KING HALL: Big banks have delivered their Q2 earnings. And the landscape is better than expected. Higher interest rates boosted the bottom line for many large lenders, though. Other income streams, like investment banking took a sizeable hit.So what's the smart financial play for your portfolio? Jon Curran, principal asset management portfolio manager, joining us now. So what is the smart play in light of all the results that we have received, Jon?JON CURRAN: Well, good morning. It's great to be with you. I think the smart play here is to stay in the large liquid diversified banks that have a nice blend of fee and interest income in their top line.I think the results really highlight the importance of diversification. And the big banks have shown themselves to be a bright spot. And that they're resilient. And their deft handling the deposit rates amidst the higher rates.JULIE HYMAN: Hey, John. It's Julie here. So in your portfolio, which of these do you hold the most of? Or what are you adding to right now?JON CURRAN: Well, we work on the bond side. And we look for the large liquid balance sheets, good access to funding, not just on the deposit side, but on the access to the debt markets. And one of the big surprises this year, one of the wild cards has been the debt issuance, which last year in 2022, January saw a $29 billion of debt issuance. This January is $9 billion.This quarter, really, is the first quarter of material bond issuance. And we've seen a lot of it. So we're looking for the banks that have durable deposit bases, but that also can access wholesale funding markets and have the investor receptivity that they do.Story continuesDIANE KING HALL: And Jon, then who would you be dumping in light of that when you use your investment thesis?JON CURRAN: So I think general good diligence wins the day here when you're considering bank investments. It's really important to do your homework, know the management teams, know that they're making good underwriting decisions. There are headwinds on the horizon. The recent fed loan officer survey did show some contraction in lending standards and lending overall.But the big banks have been very resilient in passing through some of those rates, in the form of loans to their customers while lagging the increase in deposits. They can do that because they're blessed with these large deposit bases.JULIE HYMAN: What about the non-big banks, Jon? We heard from some of the regionals today. And it looks like that, by and large, they're holding on, or even in some cases growing their deposit bases. They're having to pay up to do so. Is the debt of those banks as attractive?JON CURRAN: Well, I think I think you make a very good point. I think the recent results of the big banks really shows the widening gulf between the haves and the have-nots, the gigantic banks, the money center banks, which are positioned very well to withstand headwinds and any turbulence that may be coming down the pike, and the smaller regional banks.It was heartening to see some of the really large regional banks like PNC, Truist and US Bancorp come to market in June. That opened the gate for regional banks. But we haven't seen regional banks writ large be able to access the debt markets yet. So I think we need to just see a bit more earnings stability and a little bit more how firm or how well footed their deposit bases are before we get some sense that they can persist with success like their large bank peers.DIANE KING HALL: Jon, with more regulation coming down the pike, pretty much imminent, are you expecting to see more consolidation? And who do you see in the-- like we saw JP Morgan Chase getting bigger recently because of that consolidation. Who do you see being a target in that situation?JON CURRAN: It's an excellent question to see where the next tie-ups will occur. I think you have to look for symbiotic deposit footprints that are complementary in nature. You did see the 2019 merger between BB&T and Suntrust to form Truist. To have a transformational merger like that might make sense, but it will depend on where the deposit concentrations are the largest.But I think clearly, the large banks have shown themselves to be ones that can persevere through this environment. So the larger the banks, the more levers they have to pull, both in their top line and their funding businesses. And if you look at their concentration risks, commercial real estate is one of the headwinds out there for these banks. But the large money center banks are much more insulated. Not impervious, but more insulated than their smaller peers.JULIE HYMAN: What about just the general headwind as well from decrease in lending demand across the board, whether we're talking about businesses or individuals?JON CURRAN: We did see the contraction in some commercial and industrial, as we like to call it in the industry, C&I lending, the recent fed loan officer survey. I think that's clearly one of the headwinds that we've noted that's on the horizon.Nonetheless, JP Morgan and Wells Fargo did say that their earnings they expect to make from loans is increasing. So it's a bit of a-- on the one hand, there is probably some contraction ahead and some credit tightening. But on the other hand, there is still demand.Citigroup actually posted a surprisingly large jump in their credit card revenues. And they were the bellwether. The one thing you have to worry about or just be cautious about is if the more borrowing that occurs on plastic, the more the banks have in terms of their loans. So that's one thing we're watching, keeping a watchful eye on.JULIE HYMAN: Yeah. And indeed, we're seeing the provisioning for that kind of stuff start to creep back up once again. Jon, thanks for your perspective. Jon Curran, principal asset management portfolio manager. Appreciate it.]

Title: How banks, financial stocks could be the closest thing to a Q2 bellwether
Text: [Could bank stocks be the closest thing to a bellwether in Q2 2023 as earnings continue to roll out? Wells Fargo CIO of Wealth & Investment Management Darrell Cronk joins Yahoo Finance Live to discuss the state of the consumer and credit trends as reported by banks this week. In a note, Wells Fargo cited bank earnings to be illustrating the "true economy" while Fed officials reconsider future interest rate hikes and consumer spending remains consistent and resilient.Video TranscriptJULIE HYMAN: While earnings season has just begun, it does seem like the bellwether this quarter is shaping up to be the financials despite the sector's earlier chaos this year. For more, we're joined by Darrell Cronk, Wells Fargo CIO of wealth and Investment Management.And indeed, it has been really interesting how well the financialS-- let's leave Goldman aside for a moment. But how well they've done. And can we sort of extrapolate that out to the rest of earnings season at all?DARELL CRONK: I'd be careful, probably about extrapolating. It out I think financials have exceeded-- what I've had my eye is very closely on is both what Brian just referenced, which is the consumer and the trends. So the consumer has been resilient. The consumer always remains resilient into a slowing economy.In fact, the consumer is often the last one to kind of give up the ghost, if you will. They will spend right up to the edge of potentially a recession and jump right over the cliff into it. We're starting to see some of that in the numbers.So if you go back to the pandemic. Huge amounts of transfer payments to consumers who built big savings balances. They've ground through those savings balances. Late last year early this year, we saw big increases in credit card spending. And now, just in the last month or two, credit card spending literally dried up.Like, it went just dead silent, which is often a very late cycle indicator because it means the consumer is kind of hitting the wall, right? If they don't have the savings anymore to spend and they can't use the plastic, right? Then they stop spending at some point.Story continuesSo I think it's a really important trend to watch. We're seeing in just this quarter's earnings. We're seeing credit card delinquencies rise from a very low level but rise, nonetheless. We're seeing auto delinquencies rise from a low level but rise nonetheless. So there are some trends there that they're watching. I think, directionally, even though they're not at the normal magnitude you would expect in a late-cycle event.DIANE KING HALL: So, I feel like that's kind of the glass empty-- or glass half-empty side of the equation. It could be the-- could it be though the glass half-full side of the equation when you think about just the strength of the labor market backing up that spending that we're seeing? Sure, there's a little bit of tapering we are seeing.But again, it's not the magnitude that you would expect in terms of like what we're seeing in the financials and how these banks are holding up. We're also not seeing massive outflows. What do you make of that?DARELL CRONK: Yeah, I think that's right, Diane. And I think we've got this air pocket of labor, both firms have been resilient and not wanting to let go of their high-valued employees. But coming out of the pandemic, we had 10 million job openings and six million unemployed workers, right?We've never seen an environment like that where there was that big of a mismatch. So it's not surprising that labor has remained sticky. Now, I think what you have to parse there is-- is it labor just being sticky and not rolling over or is it that companies are robustly out there hiring today?We don't see the robust hiring side. Call it the demand side of the equation. In fact, what you really need for that to kick in is you need earnings growth and you need top line revenue growth, right? So we're going to be the second quarter in a row of negative earnings revenue growth, third quarter of negative earnings growth, and the sixth quarter in a row where we've seen margins declined.So if that environment happens and demand comes down and your single biggest cost on your income statement is labor, you would expect that if it's typical to a normal cycle, in the coming months, those layoffs would start to pick up a little bit. But you're right, the resiliency has been has been really strong.JULIE HYMAN: But is it typical to a normal cycle? I mean, the thing that kind of comes around to me as we go through each earnings season. You know, we kept talking about normalization coming out of the pandemic. And then, the conversation goes away. But, really, we're still there.I mean, when you talk about the credit card delinquencies for example. They're ticking up but they're still below where they were in 2019, which is remarkable to me. And it feels like they're all still these tension points in the economy that are not normal. Whatever normal even means anymore.DARELL CRONK: That's true.JULIE HYMAN: Right? So--DARELL CRONK: You're right, Julie.JULIE HYMAN: We're still-- what is that process still like? And how difficult does it make your job and our job to try and figure out what's going to happen?DARELL CRONK: Very difficult, right? Because if you looked at a lot of the historical indicators and the fundamental indicators. You would basically say the economy is very late cycle and probably heading to recession, which is why you had 70% of economists claiming coming into this year that the economy was going to go into a recession.That intense bed of liquidity that we just got done talking about, probably extended the duration of how a number of those normally roll over and act. But at the end of the day, the consumer is the engine of the economy, right? And labor is what will matter there.What's interesting is-- so, we all know the Fed started hiking interest rates in March of 2022, right? Very first hike at 25 basis points. The unemployment rate in March of 2022 was 3.6%. The unemployment rate today is 3.6%, right?It hasn't moved. Notwithstanding the fed has increased interest rates 500 basis points, right? So does that mean labor is different this time or this time is different? Maybe. Where you see strength in the economy. I think the important point here is you have to parse is it supply push or demand pull? Because there are two different things.If it's-- so think about, we've seen strength in labor. We've seen strength in housing. We've seen strength in travel and all those types of things. So take housing for example. People aren't lining up to buy two and three new homes. That's not happening today, right?Why is housing strong? It's strong because there's such a supply dearth, right? There's only been 1% of homes turned over this year, right? Same thing with labor. There's a dearth of labor, right? It's not that companies are running out there to hire a whole bunch of new people.Same thing in travel, right? Airlines have done what? Cut the number of flights. So if you want to go to Europe, right? This summer, you're going to pay up because there aren't the seats there.JULIE HYMAN: In that case, it feels like there's quite a lot of demand for travel though too.DARELL CRONK: There is. There's pent up demand from the pandemic, right? People just want to get back out there and do their thing again. But it's kind of colliding with this reduction in supply of what's available for seats. If you go try to find a summer seat on an airline this summer, best of luck to you, right?DIANE KING HALL: Whoa, wow, OK, I have one more flight to get to.DARELL CRONK: Yes, OK, all right, sorry, Diane.DIANE KING HALL: I better book that today.DARELL CRONK: You better get that booked.DIANE KING HALL: Exactly.]

Title: Wells Fargo & Company's (NYSE:WFC) institutional shareholders had a great week as one-year returns increased after a 5.5% gain last week
Text: [Key InsightsInstitutions' substantial holdings in Wells Fargo implies that they have significant influence over the company's share price50% of the business is held by the top 24 shareholders Analyst forecasts along with ownership data serve to give a strong idea about prospects for a businessA look at the shareholders of Wells Fargo & Company (NYSE:WFC) can tell us which group is most powerful. We can see that institutions own the lion's share in the company with 76% ownership. In other words, the group stands to gain the most (or lose the most) from their investment into the company.And as as result, institutional investors reaped the most rewards after the company's stock price gained 5.5% last week. The one-year return on investment is currently 9.4% and last week's gain would have been more than welcomed.Let's delve deeper into each type of owner of Wells Fargo, beginning with the chart below. So they generally do consider buying larger companies that are included in the relevant benchmark index.Wells Fargo already has institutions on the share registry. Indeed, they own a respectable stake in the company. This suggests some credibility amongst professional investors. But we can't rely on that fact alone since institutions make bad investments sometimes, just like everyone does. It is not uncommon to see a big share price drop if two large institutional investors try to sell out of a stock at the same time. So it is worth checking the past earnings trajectory of Wells Fargo, (below). Of course, keep in mind that there are other factors to consider, too.earnings-and-revenue-growthSince institutional investors own more than half the issued stock, the board will likely have to pay attention to their preferences. It is always good to see at least some insider ownership, but it might be worth checking if those insiders have been selling.
